title: Oil Surges Past $105 as Middle East Conflict Escalates
summary:
The price of oil has jumped to $105 a barrel amid signs the conflict in the Middle East will not be resolved quickly, fueling fears that inflation could accelerate. With fighting between the US and Iran in the Gulf intensifying, the cost of both crude oil and gas has been rising sharply. Brent crude went back above $100 a barrel on Wednesday and continued to climb.

The war has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway that normally carries oil and gas from the Gulf to global markets. US and UK long-term borrowing costs also surged to their highest level in decades.

Speaking at a Republican Party convention in Texas on Wednesday, President Trump said he did not think the fighting would end until after the US midterm elections in November. Concerns have also grown after Iran-aligned Houthi forces were reported to have seized Yemen's port of Mokha, a key Red Sea port. The move could elevate fears of further shipping disruptions.

The price of natural gas has also been soaring on wholesale markets. In the UK, it rose above 200p a therm for the first time since the end of 2022. Storage levels in Europe are much lower than normal for the time of year, and the need to fill reserves ahead of winter has helped push up prices. UK consumers are protected from short-term spikes by Ofgem's price cap, but if prices remain high for an extended period, households still face steeper bills.

The increase in energy costs has in turn raised fears of a spike in inflation, pushing up yields on government bonds around the world. In the UK, yields on 10-year bonds were at their highest since 2007, while 20- and 30-year bonds hit levels not seen since 1998. This implies a higher cost of borrowing for the government at a time when public finances are under pressure. It could also affect households directly, as it influences rates paid by consumers for products such as fixed-rate mortgages.
why_it_matters: Energy prices feed into almost everything teenagers depend on — transport, food, heating and the borrowing costs that decide whether families can afford a home. The story shows how a conflict thousands of kilometres away can reach household budgets within weeks, and how regulators and central banks try to soften the blow.

background_read: The Strait of Hormuz (a narrow sea passage between Iran and Oman) is one of the most important energy routes on Earth — a large share of the world's crude oil and natural gas travels through it by tanker, so any closure quickly raises prices everywhere. In the 1970s, an oil embargo by Arab producers cut supplies to Western countries, prices roughly quadrupled and inflation soared, an episode that still shapes how governments think about energy shocks.

The Houthis (an armed group that controls much of northern Yemen) have attacked shipping in the Red Sea in recent years, forcing many cargo and oil tankers onto much longer routes. Ofgem (the UK's energy regulator) sets a price cap limiting how much suppliers can charge households per unit of gas and electricity, which softens short-term spikes but not long ones.

Central banks such as the Bank of England and the U.S. Federal Reserve raise interest rates to slow inflation, which makes mortgages and other borrowing more expensive for families. Europe is especially exposed because it imports much of its gas and must refill storage tanks before winter, and its reserves are currently well below normal for the season.

perspectives.description: Oil and gas companies earn far more when prices climb, and producer governments collect bigger revenues. High prices can also speed up interest in renewables, though that takes years to pay off.

Higher fuel, heating and shipping costs squeeze families, and poorer households spend a bigger share of their income on energy. The UK price cap only limits short-term spikes, so a long conflict could still mean much steeper bills this winter.

They see a classic supply shock: a physical blockage of energy routes drives prices up, feeds inflation and pushes central banks to raise interest rates, which slows growth. The longer the disruption lasts, the more it spreads into the prices of other goods.

If the Strait of Hormuz stays closed and European storage remains low, winter bills and mortgage rates could rise further. Analysts will watch whether producers pump more oil, whether governments release emergency reserves, and whether the conflict widens beyond the Gulf.
